---
title: "Why plugkit exists"
subtitle: "The bug that is not a bug"
---

## Start with a bug that is not a bug

`plugkit` replaces `signalpy-kernel`, an earlier attempt at the same problem.
Understanding why it was replaced is the fastest way to understand what plugkit
does differently, so here is the old design doing exactly what it was built to
do:

```python
@component("http-server", version="1.0")
@provides("IHttpServer")
@requires(config=IConfig)
class HttpServer:
    @lifecycle.activate
    def activate(self):
        self.app = FastAPI()
        self.app.add_route("/health", self.health)

    @lifecycle.deactivate
    def deactivate(self):
        self.app = None
```

Now a second component adds a route to that server:

```python
@component("admin-api")
@requires(server=IHttpServer)
class AdminApi:
    @lifecycle.activate
    def activate(self):
        self.rt.server.app.add_route("/admin", self.handle)
```

Unload `AdminApi`. What happens to `/admin`?

It stays. Nothing recorded that `AdminApi` added it, so nothing removes it. The
route now points at a method on a component that no longer exists. `AdminApi` can
write a `deactivate` that removes it, and probably will, and will get it right
today and wrong in six months when someone adds a second route and updates only
one of the two lists.

**This is not a missing feature. It is a missing invariant.** Nothing in the old
design *owns* the undo of what a component did. So teardown is a promise each component
makes individually, and the framework cannot check it.

## The one idea in plugkit

**A registration returns its own undo, and something owns the undo.**

```python
def admin_api(ctx, config=None):
    return ctx.server.add_route("/admin", handle)   # returns a disposer
admin_api.inject = ["server"]
```

`add_route` hands back a function that removes the route. `ctx` — really the
*fiber*, the object representing this plugin's lifetime — keeps it. When the
plugin unloads, for any reason, that function is called. The component author
does not write teardown, cannot forget teardown, and cannot get teardown
half-right.

Everything else follows from that:

**Hot reload is free.** Reloading a plugin is unload-then-apply. Unload is total,
so reload is clean. There is no reload mechanism to implement.

**Dependency-driven activation is free.** If a plugin can be stopped and started
cleanly, then "stop it when its database goes away, start it when a database
appears" is just calling those two operations at the right moment.

**Swapping an implementation is free.** Replace the database service and every
plugin holding a reference to the old one is rebuilt — not patched, rebuilt —
so nobody is left holding a stale object.

## Declarative versus imperative

That is the real difference, and it is worth naming plainly.

| | signalpy | plugkit |
|---|---|---|
| A component is | a class wearing decorators | a plain class |
| Registration happens | by the kernel, reading metadata | by the plugin, calling a method |
| Teardown happens | in a `deactivate` you write | by calling the disposers you returned |
| The unit of lifetime is | a component instance | a fiber |
| Vocabulary size | 12 decorators | 4 concepts |

The old design asks you to *describe* your component and trusts the kernel to do
the right thing. plugkit asks you to *do* things and hands you the undo each
time.

The declarative version reads better in a slide. The imperative version is the
one where the framework can actually guarantee something.

## "But now my class imports the framework"

Correct, and that was the second complaint about the old design — a class covered in
`@component`, `@provides`, `@requires` is no longer a plain Python object. You
cannot construct it in a test without the kernel. You cannot lift it into another
project. It has stopped being *yours*.

plugkit's answer is to separate the component from its registration:

```python
# services/greeter.py — imports nothing. Not a framework file.
class Greeter:
    def __init__(self, database, prefix="hello"):
        self.database = database
        self.prefix = prefix

    def hello(self, name):
        return f"{self.prefix} {name}"
```

```python
# app.py — the only file that knows a kernel exists
from plugkit import provide
from services.greeter import Greeter

greeter = provide(Greeter, needs=["database"], config={"prefix": "greeter.prefix"})
```

`Greeter` is testable as `Greeter(database=FakeDB(), prefix="hi")`. No kernel, no
container, no fixtures. That is [chapter 2](02-popo-components.qmd).

## Where this design comes from

The kernel is a port of **Cordis**, the plugin framework underneath
[DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) — DeepSeek's
open-source agent runtime, ~457,000 lines of TypeScript across ~219 packages,
every one of them a Cordis plugin.

That matters for a practical reason rather than a prestige one. Because plugkit
matches Cordis's *semantics* — the same event names, the same dispatch modes, the
same lifetime rules — dsh's documentation stays a working specification for
anything built here. Its catalogue of 58 services, its five-stage tool pipeline,
its file-system policy events: all of it describes a substrate that means the
same thing in this kernel. A design ported from there is a design, not a
translation.

`src/plugkit/VENDORED.md` records which port was vendored, why, and what was
changed in it.
